title: The Gold of Time: from a Norman police house to the wall on the rue Fontaine
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Norman Child and the Lycée

stops.name: Tinchebray, the policeman's son
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the day is given as 19 February by Polizzotti and by the Wikipedia articles used here, while some reference works give 18 February. The discrepancy is recorded, not resolved
stops.campa: In a small town of the Orne, in the hedged bocage country of Normandy, a son is born to Louis-Justin Breton, a policeman who will later work as a clerk, and to Marguerite-Marie-Eugénie Le Gouguès. There is no money in the house and there are no books to speak of. They name him André. He will spend his adult life in Paris, issuing manifestos and excommunicating poets by name. The family is gone from Tinchebray before he can remember it, and he keeps no memory of the town.
suggested_refs: The birth register of Tinchebray, Orne, February 1896
sources: Mark Polizzotti, Revolution of the Mind: The Life of André Breton (1995)

stops.name: Pantin, the suburb of the first years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Polizzotti places the family's move to the Paris region in Breton's infancy without giving a year; 1897-01-01 stands for a span of roughly 1897 to 1907
stops.campa: The family moves up to the Paris region while André is still small and settles at Pantin, a working suburb on the northeast edge of the city, canal and factories and the great cemetery. His father clerks. The household is orderly and narrow and expects a profession of him. Paris proper is a tram ride away and is another country. What he sees of the capital he sees as a visitor, arriving from outside the old fortifications, on the side where the poor live.
suggested_refs: The Breton household at Pantin, Seine, in the first decade of the century

stops.name: Lorient, the Atlantic summers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and two versions stand unreconciled: Polizzotti gives childhood summers with relatives on the Breton coast near Lorient, while Encyclopedia.com has him raised for years in Brittany by his maternal grandfather. Neither is dated closely, and 1903 is a placeholder
stops.campa: Childhood summers are spent on the Breton coast near Lorient among his mother's people, and one account has him lodged there with his maternal grandfather for years rather than weeks. He is turned loose on an Atlantic port: rigging, rope, tidewrack, the traffic of a working harbour. He credits that coast afterwards with his first sense that ordinary places hold more than themselves, and that the marvellous is not somewhere else. The sea gets into him early. It comes back forty years later in Arcane 17, written facing a different Atlantic rock.
stops.quote: It is perhaps childhood that comes closest to one's 'real life'; childhood beyond which man has at his disposal, aside from his laissez-passer, only a few complimentary tickets.
stops.quote_source: Breton, Manifesto of Surrealism (1924), tr. Richard Seaver and Helen R. Lane
suggested_refs: The Le Gouguès family in the Morbihan; the port of Lorient before the First World War

stops.name: Lycée Chaptal, the Symbolists against medicine
stops.date_confidence: attested for the entry year, month defaulted to the start of the school year; the coordinates are 45 boulevard des Batignolles per OpenStreetMap, correcting a pin about 170 m off in one lens of this dossier
stops.campa: He enters the Lycée Chaptal on the boulevard des Batignolles, begins writing verse, and reads the Symbolists against the grain of his parents' plan for him, which is medicine. He does both at once: he takes the PCN medical preparatory certificate, in the company of a fellow student named Théodore Fraenkel, and he goes on writing. Mallarmé and Rimbaud are the private curriculum, run beside the official one. His teachers see a promising pupil. The poems he is already sending out under his own name are looking for someone to answer them.
suggested_refs: The Lycée Chaptal, 45 boulevard des Batignolles, Paris 8e

stops.name: Nantes, the ward and Jacques Vaché
stops.date_confidence: attested: French Wikipedia puts Breton at the Nantes hospital as a nurse from July 1915 and the meeting with Vaché in early 1916. One chronology in this dossier compresses both into 1916 and reverses the order with Saint-Dizier; the correction is followed here
stops.campa: Posted as an auxiliary nurse to the military hospital at Nantes, the medical student spends his war among the wounded. Early in the second year he meets a young soldier with a leg wound: Jacques Vaché, a disciple of Alfred Jarry, who draws in silence, dresses as a hussar or an airman or an English officer as the mood takes him, and holds that nothing whatever deserves enthusiasm. Vaché calls his position umour. He publishes nothing, admires nothing, and ruins Breton for the literary career Breton had been carefully preparing.
suggested_refs: The wartime hospital at Nantes; the letters of Jacques Vaché to Breton, published in 1919 as Lettres de guerre

stops.name: Saint-Dizier, the neuropsychiatric centre
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1916 by French Wikipedia, day defaulted; the Nantes posting precedes it by a year, against the sequence given in the English-language summaries
stops.campa: He is assigned to the army's neuropsychiatric centre at Saint-Dizier, among soldiers whose minds have given way under shellfire. He reads Freud there, or reads about him, and takes the ward as a laboratory: men speaking without governing what they say, delirium running with its own grammar and its own coherence, one patient insisting that the war is staged and the corpses are painted dummies. He is twenty. What the clinic offers him is not a cure for these men but a proposition about everyone, that beneath the reasoning voice another voice is talking and can be taken down.
suggested_refs: The centre de neuropsychiatrie of the Second Army at Saint-Dizier, Haute-Marne

stops.name: Val-de-Grâce, the ward and the salon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the posting, month defaulted; the introductions belong here and not to the 1913 student years where one chronology places them, Apollinaire being met in 1916 and Reverdy in 1917 per French Wikipedia
stops.campa: Back in Paris at the Val-de-Grâce military hospital he continues in the neuropsychiatric service, writing down the speech of shell-shocked patients. In the same months he is taken to Guillaume Apollinaire, who in 1917 coins the word surréaliste for the programme of his own play Les Mamelles de Tirésias, and to Pierre Reverdy, whose account of the image as two distant realities brought together Breton will still be quoting forty years later. The patients cannot stop talking. The poets are trying to learn how.
suggested_refs: Apollinaire's apartment at 202 boulevard Saint-Germain; Reverdy's review Nord-Sud, 1917-1918

stops.name: Nantes, the death of Jacques Vaché
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Jacques Vaché is found dead in a hotel room at Nantes, opium in him and another man's body beside him, aged twenty-three. Whether it is accident or suicide is never settled, and Breton, who has just lost the one person who ever made literature look ridiculous to him, decides that either verdict fits a man who held indifference as a discipline. Within the year Breton has gathered the letters Vaché sent him from the front and put them out as Lettres de guerre. The flat tone survives in him, and so does the refusal to be impressed by anything printed.
stops.quote: It is Jacques Vaché to whom I owe the most.
stops.quote_source: Breton on Vaché, English rendering quoted in Wikipedia, 'Jacques Vaché'; the French original was not reached in this research
suggested_refs: The hotel room at Nantes, 6 January 1919; Breton's 1919 edition of Vaché's Lettres de guerre

segments.name: Littérature, Dada, and the Magnetic Fields

stops.name: Paris, the founding of Littérature
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1919; this precedes Tzara's arrival in Paris, so the close Dada association dated to 1919 in one chronology of this dossier is a year early
stops.campa: With Louis Aragon and Philippe Soupault, both of them met in the war, he founds a review and calls it Littérature, a title chosen for its flatness and meant as an insult. It prints Valéry and Gide beside the recovered Poésies of Lautréamont and the last letters of Vaché, and within a year it is the address in Paris for everyone with no further use for the official culture that produced the war. Breton is twenty-three. He decides what the review prints and who is asked to write for it.
suggested_refs: The first series of Littérature, Paris, from March 1919

stops.name: Café Certa, passage de l'Opéra
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Certa as the group's regular meeting place across 1919-1921; Tzara reaches Paris in January 1920, which fixes the start of Paris Dada proper. The month here is a placeholder
stops.campa: Tristan Tzara arrives from Zurich in January and Paris Dada begins in earnest, with its headquarters in a bar inside the glass-roofed passage de l'Opéra called the Certa. Port is drunk there and the season's outrages are planned: manifestations that end in shouting, readings staged in order to be interrupted, provocations aimed at an audience that has bought tickets in the hope of being provoked. Breton takes to the scandal and tires of it quickly. Dada has nothing to propose once the shouting stops, and he is already looking for something to do the morning after.
suggested_refs: The Café Certa in the passage de l'Opéra; Aragon's Le Paysan de Paris on the same arcade

stops.name: Paris, Les Champs Magnétiques
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1920 for publication, month a placeholder; the composition sessions belong to the previous spring
stops.campa: He and Soupault shut themselves in a room and write at speed for days, with no subject agreed in advance, no rereading, each chapter pitched at a different tempo, and publish what comes out as Les Champs Magnétiques. It is the first book made by automatic writing. Neither of them yet has a name for the operation beyond an adjective borrowed from Apollinaire, and the movement it will found is four years away. The method arrives before the doctrine, and Breton insists on that order every time he is asked where Surrealism came from.
stops.quote: Write quickly, without any preconceived subject, fast enough so that you will not remember what you're writing and be tempted to reread what you have written.
stops.quote_source: Breton, Manifesto of Surrealism (1924), tr. Richard Seaver and Helen R. Lane; the instruction is written four years after the sessions it describes
suggested_refs: Les Champs Magnétiques, Paris, Au Sans Pareil, 1920
sources: Breton, Manifesto of Surrealism (1924), Seaver and Lane translation, full text on archive.org

stops.name: Rue Fontaine, the apartment and the Wall
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move in 1922 and for the marriage to Simone Kahn on 15 September 1921; note that this dossier carries two pins for 42 rue Fontaine, 48.8829/2.3323 and 48.8834/2.3346, roughly 180 m apart, unreconciled here
stops.campa: He marries Simone Kahn in September, and that winter the couple take an apartment at 42 rue Fontaine, at the foot of the Montmartre hill in Pigalle, among the cabarets and the brothels. Two rooms and a studio above them. He will live in this flat for the rest of his life, and the walls will fill: canvases, Oceanic masks, Hopi dolls, mounted insects, root shapes, manuscripts, objects carried home from the flea market at Saint-Ouen, more than five thousand things hung so that each one argues with its neighbour. He calls the arrangement the Wall.
suggested_refs: 42 rue Fontaine, Paris 9e; the inventory of the Breton collection drawn up before the 2003 sale

stops.name: Rue Fontaine, the season of sleeps
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1922-1923 as a period; individual sessions are not dated in the sources reached and the month here is a placeholder
stops.campa: Through two winters the group sits in darkened rooms and puts itself under. René Crevel brings the technique in. Robert Desnos goes furthest, dropping into trance almost on command, talking and writing and answering questions put to him from wherever he has gone, producing in that state the wordplay Breton rates above anything any of them has written awake. Breton keeps the minutes and treats the results as evidence rather than performance: the unconscious dictating in public, on demand, before witnesses. He calls a halt when the sleepers stop wanting to wake up.
stops.quote: After you have settled yourself in a place as favorable as possible to the concentration of your mind upon itself, have writing materials brought to you. Put yourself in as passive, or receptive, a state of mind as you can.
stops.quote_source: Breton, Manifesto of Surrealism (1924), 'Written Surrealist Composition, or First and Last Draft', tr. Richard Seaver and Helen R. Lane
suggested_refs: The époque des sommeils, 1922-1923; the trance transcripts printed in the new series of Littérature

segments.name: The Manifesto, the Bureau, and the Party

stops.name: Paris, the Manifeste du surréalisme
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1924, day defaulted
stops.campa: He publishes the Manifeste du surréalisme, a hundred pages that open with a complaint against realism and close on a dictionary entry he has written himself, defining Surrealism as psychic automatism in its pure state. The book gives working instructions: settle yourself somewhere favourable, make yourself passive, have writing materials brought, write faster than you can remember. A journal follows, La Révolution surréaliste. So does a group, and it is a long one: Soupault, Aragon, Éluard, Crevel, Leiris, Péret, Artaud, Desnos.
stops.quote: Surrealism is based on the belief in the superior reality of certain forms of previously neglected associations, in the omnipotence of dream, in the disinterested play of thought.
stops.quote_source: Breton, Manifesto of Surrealism (1924), tr. Richard Seaver and Helen R. Lane, verified against the full text on archive.org
suggested_refs: Manifeste du surréalisme, Paris, Éditions du Sagittaire, 1924; La Révolution surréaliste, twelve issues, 1924-1929
sources: Breton, Manifesto of Surrealism, Seaver and Lane translation

stops.name: 15 rue de Grenelle, the Bureau of Surrealist Research
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Bureau's opening in October 1924; Artaud's part in running it is taken from the general record of the movement rather than from a source in this dossier
stops.campa: A storefront office opens on the rue de Grenelle with a sign inviting the public in. Anyone may walk off the street and deposit a dream, a coincidence, a confession, an account of a chance meeting, and it is entered in a register kept for the purpose. Antonin Artaud takes a hand in running it and pushes the operation toward something nearer insurrection than research. It is a laboratory with no instruments and no experiments, keeping a record of what people volunteer when nobody has asked them a question.
stops.quote: So strong is the belief in life, in what is most fragile in life—real life, I mean—that in the end this belief is lost.
stops.quote_source: Breton, Manifesto of Surrealism (1924), opening sentence, tr. Richard Seaver and Helen R. Lane
suggested_refs: The Bureau de recherches surréalistes, 15 rue de Grenelle, Paris 7e, and its register of public depositions

stops.name: Paris, joining the Communist Party
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1927; no month is given in the sources reached and the day is defaulted
stops.campa: He joins the French Communist Party, taking part of the group with him and setting the question that will split it for the rest of the decade. Surrealism has promised a revolution of the mind, total and immediate, answerable to no committee. The organized revolution wants discipline, a line, and useful work, and regards the unconscious as a bourgeois hobby. Breton maintains that the two revolutions are one revolution and that anybody who says otherwise has misunderstood both. He will go on maintaining it for six years and lose friends on either side of the claim.
suggested_refs: The 1927 Surrealist tract Au grand jour, announcing the adhesion to the PCF

stops.name: Rue de Chéroy, the woman who calls herself Nadja
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by French Wikipedia, 'Léona Delcourt', which also fixes the site as the street by the Hôtel du Théâtre on the rue de Chéroy in the 17th, opposite the stage door of the Théâtre Hébertot. The rue Lafayette pin repeated elsewhere is the novel's own narration, about two kilometres away, and is not the documented place
stops.campa: On the fourth of October, in a street of the seventeenth arrondissement by the stage door of a theatre, he stops a young woman walking with her head up and her eyes heavily made up. She tells him her name is Nadja, because in Russian it is the beginning of the word for hope, and because it is only the beginning. Her name is Léona Camille Ghislaine Delcourt. She is twenty-four, born at Saint-André-lez-Lille, and she is in Paris without money and without protection. They will see each other over roughly ten days.
stops.quote: Don't I love her? When I am near her I am nearer things which are near her.
stops.quote_source: Breton, Nadja (1928), tr. Richard Howard; seen in a secondary reproduction of the Howard translation, the Grove Press scan on archive.org being access-restricted
suggested_refs: The Hôtel du Théâtre, rue de Chéroy, Paris 17e; Hester Albach, Léona, l'inspiratrice d'André Breton

stops.name: Tour Saint-Jacques, the walks
stops.date_confidence: narrated in Nadja rather than documented; the tower is one of the book's fixed points and the individual walks are undated within the ten days
stops.campa: They walk. The tower standing alone off the rue de Rivoli, all that survives of a demolished church, is one of the settled strange places of the city for him, somewhere he says he was pulled toward long before he could say why. Nadja reads the streets the way he wants them read, without method and without effort, finding signs where he finds them and also where he does not. He starts keeping notes and collecting photographs of the ground they have covered, and the walks turn into a book about chance behaving as though it meant something.
stops.quote: There is no use being alive if one must work. The event from which each of us is entitled to expect the revelation of his own life's meaning—that event which I may not yet have found, but on whose path I seek myself—is not earned by work.
stops.quote_source: Breton, Nadja (1928), tr. Richard Howard; seen in a secondary reproduction of the Howard translation, the primary Grove Press scan being access-restricted
suggested_refs: The Tour Saint-Jacques, Paris 4e; the photographs by Jacques-André Boiffard used in the first edition of Nadja

stops.name: Sainte-Anne, the committal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by French Wikipedia, 'Léona Delcourt'; the coordinates are the hospital at 1 rue Cabanis, correcting a pin about 620 m west in one lens of this dossier
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of March she breaks down at the Hôtel Becquerel and is taken first to the special infirmary of the Dépôt and then to Sainte-Anne. Breton has stopped seeing her by then. Three days later she is moved out of Paris to the asylum at Perray-Vaucluse, at Sainte-Geneviève-des-Bois, and the file leaves the city and leaves his hands. He is at work on the book about her, and in that book he will attack the asylums at length, as machines for manufacturing the madness they are supposed to treat. He does not visit her in one.
suggested_refs: The Sainte-Anne hospital, 1 rue Cabanis, Paris 14e; the Perray-Vaucluse asylum at Sainte-Geneviève-des-Bois

stops.name: Bailleul, the ward in the Nord
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by French Wikipedia, 'Léona Delcourt'; the widely repeated claim that she died at Sainte-Anne is false, and the spelling Delacourt found in English reference works is an error
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of May she is transferred again, north to the asylum at Bailleul in the Nord, back within a few miles of the country she came from. She stays fourteen years. She dies there on the fifteenth of January 1941, aged thirty-eight, in a France under German occupation, with no visitor recorded. The book that turned her into a figure of the marvellous is by then twelve years old and famous, and says nothing of any of this, having gone to press while she was at the beginning of her confinement.
suggested_refs: The asylum at Bailleul, Nord; the civil death record of Léona Delcourt, 15 January 1941

stops.name: Paris, the publication of Nadja
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1928; the exact publication day is not established in the sources reached and 25 May is a placeholder within the year
stops.campa: The book appears with photographs in place of description, on principle, so that nothing has to be evoked which can simply be shown: the hotel front, the shop sign, the tower, a pair of eyes. It opens by asking who am I and answers with a proverb about haunting. It closes on a sentence that outlives everything else in it and that Pierre Boulez will one day take for the title of a piece of music. The woman it is about is in a locked ward two hundred and forty kilometres north, and is named in it only as Nadja.
stops.quote: Beauty will be convulsive or will not be at all.
stops.quote_source: Breton, Nadja (1928), closing line, tr. Richard Howard; verified through a secondary reproduction of the Howard translation, the primary Grove Press scan being access-restricted
suggested_refs: Nadja, Paris, Gallimard, 1928; Boulez, ...explosante-fixe...; Mark Polizzotti's 2025 retranslation for New York Review Books

segments.name: The Second Manifesto, the Party, and Mexico

stops.name: Paris, the Second Manifesto
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1929, in the final number of La Révolution surréaliste, day defaulted; the answering pamphlet Un Cadavre is dated 1930 in this dossier
stops.campa: The Second Manifesto comes out in the last number of La Révolution surréaliste: an audit of the movement conducted name by name, expelling much of it, and carrying the sentence about the simplest surrealist act being to go down into the street with a revolver in the fist and fire at random into the crowd. The expelled answer with a pamphlet called Un Cadavre, taking the title from the one the Surrealists themselves had used over the corpse of Anatole France. They accuse Breton of running a church and of behaving in it like a priest.
suggested_refs: Second manifeste du surréalisme, La Révolution surréaliste no. 12, December 1929; Un Cadavre, Paris, 1930

stops.name: Paris, expelled from the Party
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1933; no month is given in the sources reached. Aragon's move in the opposite direction in 1932 is stated from the general record rather than from a source in this dossier
stops.campa: The French Communist Party expels him. The charge is the one always brought against him there, that he will not subordinate what he writes to what the Party requires, and the result is a revolutionary without an organization, defending in the same breath the freedom of the dream and the necessity of the class war. Louis Aragon has already gone the other way, choosing the Party, socialist realism, and a long career, and breaking with Surrealism for good. He was one of the three men who founded Littérature. The two of them do not speak again.
suggested_refs: The 1933 exclusion of Breton, Éluard, and Crevel from the PCF

stops.name: Paris, the Congress and the death of René Crevel
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Ehrenburg slap, the expulsion from the Congress, and Crevel's suicide on 18 June 1935 during the Congress are all confirmed. One chronology in this dossier softens the last of these to a phrase about being affected by the surrounding conflict, which is wrong
stops.campa: At the International Congress of Writers for the Defence of Culture the Surrealists are kept off the platform. Breton meets Ilya Ehrenburg in the street, who has disparaged them in print, and slaps him; the group is expelled from the proceedings. René Crevel has been going between the two camps trying to get them readmitted, and is treated as marginal inside his own group on account of his bisexuality. On the eighteenth of June he goes home and kills himself. He was the one who brought the sleeping sessions into the rue Fontaine thirteen years before.
suggested_refs: The Congrès international des écrivains pour la défense de la culture, Paris, June 1935

stops.name: Coyoacán, the manifesto at Trotsky's table
stops.date_confidence: attested: Breton is in Mexico from April to roughly August 1938 and the manifesto is drafted in July, correcting a narrower April-to-May window given in one lens. The coordinates are the Trotsky house on Avenida Río Churubusco per OpenStreetMap, correcting a pin about 1.9 km away
stops.campa: Sent to Mexico on a cultural commission, he is taken in by Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo and driven out to the guarded house where Leon Trotsky is living. The two men talk for months, quarrel, walk, fish, and draft together a manifesto for an independent revolutionary art whose demand is complete freedom for art and no orders from any state whatever. Trotsky writes much of it and then takes his name off it; it goes out signed by Breton and Rivera. Breton tells Kahlo she is a surrealist who arrived at it without having heard the word.
suggested_refs: Pour un art révolutionnaire indépendant, Mexico, July 1938; the Museo Casa de León Trotsky, Coyoacán
sources: diego_rivera.journey.json and frida_kahlo.journey.json (1938 Breton and Trotsky stops)

stops.name: Paris, the Mexique exhibition
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1939 for the exhibition and to January 1939 for Kahlo's arrival; the coordinates are inherited unchanged from the Kahlo file of this corpus
stops.campa: Frida Kahlo sails for Paris in January on his promise of an exhibition and arrives to find the household without money and her canvases held in customs. It is Marcel Duchamp, not Breton, who gets the show hung in March, the paintings put up among pre-Columbian figures and painted retablos under the title Mexique. Breton writes the catalogue text and repeats the line he gave her in Coyoacán. She spends much of the rest of her life refusing the label, and says she never painted dreams, only her own life.
suggested_refs: Mexique, Galerie Renou et Colle, Paris, March 1939, and Breton's catalogue preface

stops.name: Villa Air-Bel, waiting for papers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence across 1940-41, month a placeholder; the pin is the La Pomme quarter of the 11th arrondissement, about 1.4 km north of a coordinate given elsewhere in this dossier. The Vichy phrase about the negation of the national revolution survives only in Franklin Rosemont's English rendering, no primary decree having been traced, so it is not set here as a quotation
stops.campa: Vichy has banned his writings as a negation of the national revolution. He is at Marseille with his wife Jacqueline Lamba and their daughter Aube, in a large cold house in the La Pomme quarter where Varian Fry's Emergency Rescue Committee parks its artists while their papers are worked on. Twenty people wait there for visas that may never be granted. To pass the time they play the exquisite corpse, hold mock auctions of the results, hang canvases in the plane trees on Sundays, and invent card games. The police search the house during a visit by Marshal Pétain to the city.
suggested_refs: Villa Air-Bel, La Pomme, Marseille; Rosemary Sullivan, Villa Air-Bel (2006)
sources: Franklin Rosemont, André Breton and the First Principles of Surrealism (1978)

stops.name: Marseille, the Capitaine Paul-Lemerle sails
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia gives 25 March 1941; one lens of this dossier gives 24 March for the same sailing, and the discrepancy is left open. The ship's name rests on non-encyclopedic sources, though the sailing in company with Lam and Lévi-Strauss is independently confirmed. The pin is this corpus's Marseille coordinate, inherited unchanged
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of March a cargo ship clears Marseille with several hundred people aboard, rated for a handful of passengers, the rest sleeping in the hold on straw laid over the bilge. Wifredo Lam is aboard, who has spent the winter drawing the plates for Breton's poem Fata Morgana. So is Victor Serge, wanted by two states. So is a young ethnographer named Claude Lévi-Strauss, who will put this voyage at the head of Tristes Tropiques. The Vichy authorities let them go on the understanding that they are somebody else's problem now.
suggested_refs: The Capitaine Paul-Lemerle, Marseille to Martinique, March 1941; Lévi-Strauss, Tristes Tropiques (1955), opening chapters

stops.name: The Lazaret, Martinique: interned on arrival
stops.date_confidence: attested for the April 1941 internment, day defaulted; the pin is inherited byte for byte from the Lévi-Strauss file of this corpus, which places the quarantine station across the bay from Fort-de-France
stops.campa: The ship puts in at Fort-de-France and the Vichy colonial administration marches the refugees across the bay to the Lazaret, a former leper station, where they are held under guard while their politics are examined at leisure. Breton is questioned as a suspect: a Frenchman traveling with a trunk of unpublished manuscripts, on an island whose garrison is loyal to Pétain and whose shops are empty. Claude Lévi-Strauss is held with him. After some weeks he is released on caution and allowed into the town.
suggested_refs: The Lazaret quarantine station, Baie de Fort-de-France, Martinique, 1941

stops.name: Fort-de-France, the haberdashery and Aimé Césaire
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1941 stopover, the day within April being a placeholder; the English Wikipedia article on Césaire dates the meeting to 1940 and places it in New York, both impossible given the 25 March 1941 sailing, and that page is treated here as in error
stops.campa: Looking for a ribbon for his daughter in a haberdasher's shop in the town, he takes a magazine down from a shelf and reads two pages of it standing at the counter. It is Tropiques, edited by Aimé Césaire, Suzanne Césaire, René Ménil, and Aristide Maugée, printed under the censor's eye on an island where there is no paper and no ink to spare. He asks who the editor is and is told he teaches at the lycée. The poem Césaire puts into his hands is Cahier d'un retour au pays natal, and Breton will carry it into the world.
suggested_refs: Tropiques, Fort-de-France, 1941-1945; Breton, Martinique charmeuse de serpents (1948)

stops.name: San Juan, the papers examined again
stops.date_confidence: attested for the refugee route as a whole and inherited from the Lévi-Strauss file of this corpus; the Ciudad Trujillo leg is a reconstruction from Polizzotti and is not separately corroborated here
stops.campa: The passage north runs through the Caribbean by whatever route the war permits, and the refugees are put ashore again at San Juan, where American officials go through the party's papers at length. Some accounts route Breton through Ciudad Trujillo as well, one more stopover on a crossing that has taken two months to cover a distance a liner used to manage in six days. He is out of France and not yet anywhere, holding a transit visa and a poem by a schoolteacher from Martinique.
suggested_refs: The Antilles route of the 1941 refugee crossings, Martinique to Puerto Rico to New York

stops.name: New York, landfall
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by French Wikipedia; Breton's refusal to learn English is reported in the general literature rather than in a source reached here
stops.campa: He lands in New York on the fourteenth of July, having got clear of France with the help of Varian Fry and of the American vice-consul Hiram Bingham, who issued visas his own government did not want issued. The city already holds Max Ernst, Marcel Duchamp, Yves Tanguy, and Peggy Guggenheim's money. Breton declines to learn English for the whole of his stay, on the ground that it would spoil his French, and lives inside the language he brought with him. He is forty-five, and the movement he commands is scattered over two continents.
suggested_refs: The Emergency Rescue Committee lists; Hiram Bingham IV's visa records at the Marseille consulate

stops.name: New Haven, the Yale exhibition and Fata Morgana
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1942 for both the exhibition and the publication, month defaulted. The claim that Breton met Lam en route through Martinique is false: they met in Paris in 1939, and the Fata Morgana drawings were made at Marseille in 1940-41, before the crossing
stops.campa: He organizes a Surrealist exhibition at Yale and speaks to the students there. The same year Fata Morgana appears with Wifredo Lam's drawings, a long poem written at Marseille in the months of waiting and illustrated there by a painter Breton had known in Paris since 1939 and who then sailed with him. Vichy's censors had refused the poem publication in France. It comes out in the Americas instead, which is where its author and its illustrator both are, and where its language has almost no readers.
suggested_refs: Fata Morgana, Buenos Aires, 1942, with drawings by Wifredo Lam

stops.name: New York, the review VVV
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1942-1944 for the review's run, month a placeholder; the gloss on the title is given in the first issue and is reported here from the general record
stops.campa: A foreign national may not hold the editorship, so the young sculptor David Hare is put at the head of it, with Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp advising and Breton directing everything that matters. They call it VVV, and the first issue explains the three letters at length and in several directions at once. Four numbers appear in three years, printed on emigre money, in a city where most of the neighbours cannot read the language. It is enough to keep the movement in existence on paper while its members are dispersed over two hemispheres.
suggested_refs: VVV, New York, four issues, 1942-1944; the parallel review View, edited by Charles Henri Ford

stops.name: 451 Madison Avenue, First Papers of Surrealism
stops.date_confidence: attested for the venue, the Whitelaw Reid Mansion, correcting a conflation with Peggy Guggenheim's Art of This Century, which opened the same season at 30 West 57th Street. Duchamp's twine and the children at the opening are reported in the general record of the exhibition
stops.campa: The exhibition Breton assembles with Marcel Duchamp opens in the ballroom of an old mansion on Madison Avenue, hung for the benefit of French war relief. Duchamp strings a mile of twine back and forth across the rooms so that the paintings can hardly be approached, and arranges for children to play ball in the galleries on the opening night and to tell any adult who objects that they were given permission. The title is taken from the immigration paperwork of a first application for American citizenship.
suggested_refs: First Papers of Surrealism, Whitelaw Reid Mansion, 451 Madison Avenue, New York, October 1942

stops.name: New York, Elisa
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1943 for the meeting, month defaulted; the Reno divorce is a reconstruction from Polizzotti and is not separately corroborated
stops.campa: The marriage to Jacqueline Lamba ends, she having gone to David Hare, and the decree is taken out in Nevada where the law is quick about it. In New York he meets a Chilean woman named Elisa Bindhoff. She is with him for the rest of his life and he marries her once the war is over. The writing about love he does from here on is not the convulsive kind that made Nadja: it is addressed to one person who is in the room. Within a year he is writing Arcane 17 in front of her, and she is in it.
suggested_refs: Elisa Bindhoff Enet, third wife of Breton and guardian of the rue Fontaine collection after his death

stops.name: Percé, Gaspé: Arcane 17
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1944 for the Gaspé stay; the Maine and Laurentian legs of the same summer are reconstructions from Polizzotti and are not given stops here
stops.campa: He travels with Elisa to the Gaspé Peninsula and to the village of Percé, where a wall of limestone stands offshore with a hole driven through it by the sea and the tide uncovers a path to it twice a day. Facing that rock he writes Arcane 17: on Melusina, on the tarot, on the war he is sitting out at a distance of four thousand kilometres, on the friends dead in Europe, and on the proposition that the world will not be repaired by men, who have had the government of it and have shown what they can do.
suggested_refs: Arcane 17, New York, Brentano's, 1945; the Rocher Percé, Gaspésie

stops.name: Port-au-Prince, the lectures and La Ruche
stops.date_confidence: attested for the visit and for the effect as the sources credit it; the causal line from the lectures to the fall of Lescot in January 1946 is how those sources report the sequence, not a demonstrated cause
stops.campa: He lectures in Haiti in the last December of the war, in a country where a Vodou-practicing countryside, the memory of nineteen years of American occupation, and a French-educated elite have been at odds for a generation. He speaks about Surrealism, about freedom, and about the Haitian Revolution as unfinished business. The students of the journal La Ruche print the lecture, the government of Élie Lescot seizes the issue, a general strike follows, and within weeks the government falls. He also finds Hector Hyppolite, a Vodou priest who paints, and says so loudly.
suggested_refs: La Ruche, Port-au-Prince, December 1945; the paintings of Hector Hyppolite at the Centre d'Art

stops.name: Le Havre, coming back
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by French Wikipedia
stops.campa: He lands at Le Havre on the twenty-fifth of May, five years out of the country, in a France where the men who stayed hold the moral authority and the word of the hour is engagement. Existentialism is what Paris is reading. Surrealism is spoken of in the past tense, as something that happened between the wars, by people who were schoolchildren while it happened. Breton is fifty years old and intends to begin again with whoever will come. A good many of the young do come, and most of them are eventually shown the door.
suggested_refs: The postwar reconstitution of the Surrealist group in Paris, 1946-1950

stops.name: Paris, the homage to Antonin Artaud
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1946 for Breton's part in the tributes; the exact day is a placeholder within the month
stops.campa: Within weeks of landing he takes part in the tributes got up for Antonin Artaud, just out of nine years in asylums, starved down to nothing and preparing the readings at the Vieux-Colombier and the Sarah Bernhardt that will be talked about for fifty years. Breton had excommunicated him from the group two decades earlier in the tract Au grand jour, and Surrealists had gone to heckle his theatre. He speaks for him now, and helps raise money for him. Neither man retracts a word of the old quarrel.
suggested_refs: The 1946 Paris benefit and homage for Artaud; Artaud's Vieux-Colombier lecture, January 1947
sources: artaud.journey.json (Au grand jour, Théâtre Alfred Jarry, and 1946 homage stops)

stops.name: Saint-Cirq-Lapopie, the house above the Lot
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1951 for the purchase, month a placeholder; the coordinates are the village per OpenStreetMap, and this dossier carries three different pins for the same house, up to about a kilometre apart
stops.campa: He buys a house in a village standing on a cliff above the Lot, a place of half-ruined medieval fronts that painters had found before him and that was close to being abandoned. He writes that on his first evening there he stopped wishing to be anywhere else. He comes back every summer for fifteen years, walks the limestone causse, gathers agates out of the riverbed, and holds a kind of open court for anybody who makes the journey down. The Paris winters go on producing quarrels and expulsions. The summers here produce stones.
suggested_refs: Breton's house at Saint-Cirq-Lapopie, Lot, bought in 1951

stops.name: Paris, the Manifesto of the 121
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1960 for Breton's signature; 6 September is the declaration's publication date and is used here to place it in the year. The 1925 tract against the Rif war is mentioned from the general record rather than from a source in this dossier
stops.campa: He signs the Declaration on the right of insubordination in the war in Algeria: a hundred and twenty-one writers, teachers, and artists asserting that a Frenchman may refuse to bear arms against the Algerian people and that those who help the Algerians are justified in doing it. Signatories lose state posts, are barred from radio and television, and several are prosecuted. He is sixty-four. He has been putting his name to papers of this kind since 1925, when the group's first political act was against the war in Morocco.
suggested_refs: Déclaration sur le droit à l'insoumission dans la guerre d'Algérie, September 1960; the review La Brèche, founded 1961

stops.name: Hôpital Lariboisière, the last day
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by French Wikipedia, which gives respiratory failure as the cause and Saint-Cirq-Lapopie as the place he was brought from
stops.campa: He is taken ill at Saint-Cirq-Lapopie in September and brought up to Paris, to the Lariboisière, where he dies of respiratory failure on the twenty-eighth at the age of seventy. He had led one movement for forty-two years and had written its definition himself, in the form of a dictionary entry. He had outlived by decades the first announcements that it was finished. Elisa and his daughter Aube leave the apartment on the rue Fontaine exactly as it stands, and it stays that way for thirty-seven years.
stops.quote: Perhaps my life is nothing but an image of this kind; perhaps I am doomed to retrace my steps under the illusion that I am exploring, doomed to try and learn what I simply should recognize, learning a mere fraction of what I have forgotten.
stops.quote_source: Breton, Nadja (1928), tr. Richard Howard; seen in a secondary reproduction of the Howard translation, the primary Grove Press scan being access-restricted
suggested_refs: The Hôpital Lariboisière, Paris 10e

stops.name: Cimetière des Batignolles, the starred octahedron
stops.date_confidence: attested for the cemetery and the 31st division; the burial day is not established in the sources reached. The coordinates are the cemetery per OpenStreetMap, and this dossier carries three separate pins for the same grave, up to about a kilometre apart
stops.campa: He is buried in the thirty-first division of the cemetery at Batignolles, in the arrondissement where his lycée stood and where he once stopped a woman in the street. The stone is cut as a starred octahedron, a crystal, the form he had held up all his life as the model of a work that grows by its own law and owes nothing to anybody's intention. The epitaph is a line of his own. Léona Delcourt has been dead twenty-five years in a ward in the Nord. Jacques Vaché has been dead forty-seven.
stops.quote_source: Epitaph on Breton's tomb, Cimetière des Batignolles, cited in French Wikipedia, 'André Breton'
suggested_refs: Breton's tomb, 31st division, Cimetière des Batignolles, Paris 17e

stops.name: Centre Pompidou, the wall rebuilt
stops.date_confidence: the venue and the fact of the Drouot-Richelieu sale are attested; the April 2003 date is press-reported and could not be confirmed in the sources reached, a French page on the sale returning a 404
stops.campa: The rue Fontaine collection is sold at Drouot-Richelieu, his widow Elisa and his daughter Aube having kept it whole for decades: more than five thousand lots, masks, canvases, letters, beetles, stones, root shapes, dispersed over several days to buyers on four continents. He had been forced to auction an earlier collection in 1931 and had built this one back. One wall is saved entire and rebuilt behind glass at the Pompidou, every object in the place he put it. The sale runs ten days and takes in more than forty-six million euros, half again what it had been expected to fetch.
suggested_refs: Le Mur de l'atelier d'André Breton, Musée national d'art moderne, Centre Georges Pompidou
